{{Short description|German physicist}}
'''Dieter Haidt''' (born 1940) is a German physicist, known for his contribution to the 1973 discovery of [[weak neutral current]]s.<ref name=CERNnews>{{cite journal|title=Italian Physical Societs honours Gargamelle physicists with Fermi award|journal=CERN Courier|date=November 2011|page=42|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1734726/files/vol51-issue9-p042-e.pdf}}</ref><ref name=DESYnews>{{cite web|url=https://www.desy.de/news/news_search/index_eng.html?openDirectAnchor=344&two_columns=0 | website=News from the DESY research centre|title=Dieter Haidt wins Enrico Fermi Prize |date=23 September 2011}}</ref> The discovery was made in the [[Gargamelle]] experiment, which used a [[heavy liquid]] [[bubble chamber]] [[detector]] in operation at [[CERN]] from 1970 to 1979.<ref>{{cite web|author=Haidt, Dieter|title=The neutrino's 50th birthday|website=Deutsches Elektyronen-Synchrotron DESY (desy.org)|url=https://www.desy.de/~haidt/nove06.pdf}}</ref>

==Education and career==
In 1958 Haidt graduated from the Kepler-Gymnasium in [[Tübingen]]. He then studied physics at the [[University of Tübingen]], where he graduated with a ''[[Diplom]]'' in experimental physics in 1965. He then moved to [[RWTH Aachen University]], where he was a member of the X2 collaboration.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Dieter Haidt's Web Page|website=desy.de|url=https://www.desy.de/~haidt/}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Esveld, C.D.|year=1973|title=An experimental study of K<sup>+</sup><sub>e<sup>4</sup></sub> decay (No. INIS-MF--1012)|publisher=Katholieke Universiteit Nijmegen (Netherlands)|url=https://inis.iaea.org/collection/NCLCollectionStore/_Public/05/099/5099942.pdf}} (See pp. 1–3.)</ref> He was also a visiting scholar at [[University College London]] in 1966. In 1969 he received his doctorate at RWTH Aachen University ''summa cum laude''<ref name=CV/><ref>{{cite book | last=Haidt | first=D. | title=Messung der Formfaktoren aus den Spektren des Zerfalls K<sup>+</sup> → π°μ+γμ | year=1970 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9FLCzQEACAAJ | language=de |postscript=; doctoral dissertation}} (Measurement of the form factors from the spectra of the decay of a positively charged [[kaon]] into a [[pion]] pair.)</ref> and in 1970 he received the Borchers Medal. From 1970 he was a member of the [[Gargamelle]] collaboration at [[CERN]] (from RWTH Aachen University) and from 1971 to 1978 he was employed at CERN.<ref name=CV/> In 1973, the Gargamelle collaboration discovered weak neutral currents.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Haidt, Dieter|url=https://cerncourier.com/a/the-discovery-of-the-weak-neutral-currents/ |title=The discovery of the weak neutral currents |volume=55|issue=8|date=3 October 2004 |journal=CERN Courier}} (reprinted: {{cite journal|title=The discovery of the weak neutral currents|journal=AAPPS Bulletin|date=February 2005|volume=15|issue=1|pages=47–50|
url=https://fwe.ifj.edu.pl/uploads/Seminaria/neutral_current/3_bubble_chambers.pdf}})</ref> The collaboration searched for weak neutral currents in neutrino reactions without muon generation. The discovery's rapid recognition depended, to a considerable extent, on calculations by Haidt, who showed that the existence of weak neutral currents was a new type of effect (and not, ''e.g.'', interactions between neutrons).<ref name=DESYnews/><ref name=CV/> Other prominent physicists involved in the Gargamelle experiment include [[Antonino Pullia]] (1935–2020), [[Helmut Faissner]] (1928–2007), and [[André Lagarrigue]] (1924–1975).<ref name="Hasert Faissner Krenz Von Krogh 1973 pp. 121–124">{{cite journal | last1=Hasert | first1=F.J. | last2=Faissner | first2=H. | last3=Krenz | Haidt was a spokesperson for the neutrino-propane experiment at the Gargamelle bubble chamber. He was involved in neutrino experiments at the BEBC detector. From 1979 to 2004 he was a senior scientist at [[DESY]]. From 1979 to 1986 he was a member of the JADE collaboration at DESY and from 1994 of the H1 collaboration. He was a member of the Physics Research Committee (PRC) at DESY and organized the DESY seminars. In 2007 he received emeritus status.<ref name=CV/>

For the academic year 1987–1988 he was a visiting scientist at Japanese particle physics laboratory known as [[KEK]].<ref name=CV/>

In 2011 he shared the [[Enrico Fermi Prize]] with Antonino Pullia.<ref name=CERNnews/><ref name=DESYnews/> In 2009, the Gargamelle collaboration received the European Physical Society's High-Energy and Particle Physics Prize.<ref name=CERNnews/>

From 1986 to 1997 he was an editor for the [[Zeitschrift für Physik|''Zeitschrift für Physik C'']] and from 1997 to 2006 he was the editor-in-chief of its successor, the ''[[European Physical Journal C]]''.<ref name=CV/>
